exercises.question: White to move. Black has just grabbed the pawn on b2 and attacks your queen. Find checkmate in one move.
exercises.explanation: Checkmate ends the game at once, so the attack on your queen does not matter. After Rd8+ the black king cannot escape because its own pawns block f7, g7 and h7, nothing can block on e8 or f8, and nothing can capture the rook: the bishop on c8 blocks the rook on a8.

wrong.why: Wins the queen, but Rd8 was checkmate; always look for checks before you take material.

exercises.hint: Which checks do you have? Look at the black king's back rank.
exercises.objective: Recognize that checkmate beats any material gain, and check every check first.

exercises.question: Black to move. Find checkmate in one move.
exercises.explanation: The queen goes down the open g-file and captures on g2 with check. The white king cannot take the queen because the knight on f4 defends g2, and every escape square (f1, h1, h2) is covered by the queen. A king can never capture a protected piece.

wrong.why: A check, but after gxh3 or Kf1 the game goes on; Qxg2 ended it.

exercises.hint: Can the king capture a piece that is defended?
exercises.objective: Deliver a queen mate supported by another piece.

exercises.question: White to move. Black has just played ...d7-d5. Win material.
exercises.explanation: Black's pawn passed over d6, so your e5-pawn may capture it en passant, but only on this move. The pawn lands on d6 and attacks both the queen on e7 and the knight on c7. If the queen takes on d6, Qxd6 wins it, because your queen on d1 guards d6 down the open file. So the queen must move away and you collect the knight.

wrong.why: Chases the bishop but lets the en passant chance disappear forever.
Attacks the queen, but the queen simply moves and the chance to capture en passant is gone.

exercises.hint: Which pawn just moved two squares, and which of your pawns stands next to it?
exercises.objective: Spot an en passant capture and use it immediately.

exercises.question: Black to move. White has just played e2-e4. What is the strongest move?
exercises.explanation: Your d4-pawn is on Black's fifth rank (the fourth rank on the board), and White's pawn has just passed e3, so you may capture en passant. The pawn lands on e3 with check and also attacks the rook on d2. The king cannot take on e3 because your rook on e8 now guards it along the open e-file. White loses the rook.

wrong.why: Wins a pawn, but taking en passant wins a whole rook.
A quiet move that lets the en passant chance slip away.

exercises.hint: En passant works for Black too, from the fourth rank.
exercises.objective: Use en passant as a forcing move that gives check and forks.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's bishop on b7 attacks your rook on h1. Are you still allowed to castle? Find a move that looks after both the rook and the king.
exercises.explanation: Castling is legal: the king has not moved, f1 and g1 are empty and not attacked, and the king is not in check. An attacked rook does not stop castling. O-O moves the rook out of the bishop's line and tucks your king away in one move, and g2 can be covered later by Bf3 or f3 if needed. Moving the rook to g1 also saves it, but leaves your king in the centre.

wrong.why: Castles the wrong way: the rook on h1 is still attacked and Black wins the exchange with ...Bxh1.
Develops, but ignores the threat, and ...Bxh1 wins a whole rook.

exercises.hint: Which piece moves when you castle kingside?
exercises.objective: Know that an attacked rook may castle, and use castling to solve two problems at once.

exercises.question: Black to move. White has just played Qa4+, checking your king and attacking your bishop on g4. Castling is not allowed while you are in check. What is the best way out?
exercises.explanation: You must deal with the check, and you cannot castle out of it. Look for a block that also saves the attacked bishop: Bd7 does both, because the bishop retreats along the g4-d7 diagonal into the line of the check. Your castling rights are untouched because the king did not move. Blocks with the knights or the c-pawn leave the bishop on g4 hanging to Qxg4.

wrong.why: Blocks the check, but Qxg4 wins the bishop for nothing.
Blocks the check, but the bishop on g4 is still undefended and falls to Qxg4.
Saves the bishop, but after Bb5 the queen is pinned and Black loses material.

exercises.hint: Which block also moves the attacked piece to safety?
exercises.objective: Escape check in the way that also solves the second threat, and know that blocking keeps your castling rights.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's queen threatens ...Qe1, which would be checkmate. You can promote your pawn. Which piece should it become?
exercises.explanation: A new queen on c8 would give no check, and Black would mate you with ...Qe1. A knight on c8 gives check to the king on d6 and attacks the queen on e7 at the same time. Black must answer the check, and then you take the queen, leaving you a bishop up with an easily winning endgame.

wrong.why: No check, so Black plays ...Qe1, which is checkmate.
Makes room for the king, but Black simply takes your pawn with ...Kxc7 or ...Qxc7 and is a queen up.

exercises.hint: Which new piece would give check?
exercises.objective: Underpromote to a knight when the knight's check or fork is worth more than a queen.

exercises.question: Black to move. White's king attacks your pawn on g2, so you must promote now. Which piece should it become?
exercises.explanation: Count the white king's squares after each promotion. A queen on g1 would cover g2, g3 and h2, while your king covers g4 and h4: White would have no legal move and no check, which is stalemate. A rook covers the g-file and the first rank but not h2, so White still has a move, and King and Rook against King is a forced win.

wrong.why: Stalemate: White has no legal move, and the game is drawn on the spot.
Avoids stalemate but loses the pawn to Kxg2, and the blocked a-pawns give a draw.

exercises.hint: After a queen promotion, where could the white king go?
exercises.objective: Underpromote to a rook to avoid stalemate.

exercises.question: White to move. Black has only a king and blocked pawns. Finish the game, and be careful.
exercises.explanation: Black's pawns cannot move, so Black's only possible moves are king moves. Qg7 gives check, and the queen is defended by your king, so it is mate. The natural-looking Qg6 takes away g8, g7 and h7 without giving check, and Black has no legal move at all: stalemate.

wrong.why: Stalemate: Black is not in check and has no legal move, so the game is a draw.

exercises.hint: Can Black move any pawn? Then look for a check.
exercises.objective: Avoid stalemate by checking whether the opponent has a legal move.

exercises.question: Black to move. You are a rook down and White is threatening to win more. Which move saves the game?
exercises.explanation: Look for checks: the white king has no shelter on the dark squares f4 and c1. After Qf4+ the king can only go to g1 or h1, and Qc1+ (or Qf1+) drives it back. If White blocks with g3, Qxf2+ keeps checking. The same position will repeat three times, which is a draw by repetition.

wrong.why: Defends nothing important and gives White time to attack with Qb8 or Rxf7; Black is lost.
A quiet move; White's queen and rook pick off pawns and mate soon follows.

exercises.hint: When you are losing, look for checks that never run out.
exercises.objective: Save a lost position with perpetual check and threefold repetition.

exercises.question: White to move. Black has just played ...g7-g5. Find checkmate in one move.
exercises.explanation: Your h5-pawn may capture the g5-pawn en passant, landing on g6. That move also clears the h-file, so the rook on h1 gives check. The king cannot take on g6 (the f5-pawn guards it), g7 and g5 are covered by the knight, and h7 and h5 are on the rook's file. Capturing with the other pawn, fxg6, gives no check.

wrong.why: Also captures en passant, but the h-file stays closed, so there is no check.

exercises.hint: Which en passant capture opens a line for your rook?
exercises.objective: See en passant as a move that can open lines and deliver a discovered check.
